5c51f4ae9b:
The guide lists four things for this objective: structured output, validation, defensive parsing, and skepticism of confident output. This chapter treats every model response as untrusted input to the rest of your system. It covers:

  • how to constrain the shape of a response: JSON outputs through output_config.format, strict tool use, and a tool used purely as an extraction contract;
  • what those guarantees cover and what they don't;
  • the supported JSON Schema subset and its limits;
  • schema design that stops the model from filling gaps with invented values (nullable fields, enums with unclear and other);
  • validation layers, from Pydantic and Jackson with Bean Validation through business rules and cross-field arithmetic;
  • defensive parsing of free text and stop_reason handling;
  • retry with error feedback, and the cases where retry can't help;
  • verification passes, grounding quotes and the problem of uncalibrated confidence.

It ends with one extraction pipeline built end to end. The same material is CCAR-F task statements 4.3 and 4.4, so this chapter serves both exams.
97da60f559: Neighbouring chapters: chapter 05 owns the Messages API request and response shape, tool_choice and the prefill removal. Chapter 12 owns error recovery in general: backoff, fallback models, circuit breakers, continuation of truncated prose, streaming refusals. This chapter only adds what is specific to structured output. Chapter 17 covers prompt techniques such as few-shot examples. Chapter 21 covers tool implementation, dispatch and tool errors. Chapter 07 covers batch processing of extraction jobs.
17547e122d:
At 2.6% of 53 items, the objective is worth one or two direct questions. But the reasoning shows up inside scenario questions across the exam. Watch for anything about extraction, classification, agents that write to systems of record, or "the output looked right but was wrong".

A wrong option usually takes one of three shapes:

  • a prompt-only fix for a guarantee that needs code ("tell the model to always output valid JSON");
  • a retry for a problem that isn't a misreading (the data isn't in the document);
  • trust in a number the model produced about itself (a confidence score).

The right option usually moves a guarantee out of the prompt, into the schema or into deterministic code. And it gives uncertainty an explicit place to go.
70d92e9e4f: Almost every idea in this chapter predates language models. What's new is the producer of the data. It never returns a type error, and once constrained it rarely returns malformed output. Yet it can still return a well-formed, plausible, wrong value. The lineage helps on the exam, because the distractors are usually ideas that were right for the old producer and wrong for this one.
d7375a5a8a:
The robustness principle. Jon Postel's rule for TCP (RFC 761, 1980) was "be conservative in what you do, be liberal in what you accept from others". It made early Internet protocols interoperate. It also made them hard to secure, because a liberal parser accepts inputs its authors never thought about.

The modern correction, argued in RFC 9413 (2023), is to be precise about what you accept and to reject the rest loudly. Defensive parsing of model text follows the corrected version. Extract by an agreed delimiter, accept exactly one well-formed value, and reject anything you would have to guess about.
871d7a0371: Schemas as contracts. XML Schema (2001) and then JSON Schema (drafts from 2009, the 2020-12 draft today) let two systems agree on the shape of a document and check it mechanically. OpenAPI made the same schemas the contract for REST APIs. The Claude API accepts JSON Schema in two places: as the input_schema of a tool, and as the schema of a JSON output. So the vocabulary is the one you already use for service contracts.
a345aca091:
Validation as a layer. Bean Validation (JSR 303, 2009; now Jakarta Validation) gave the JVM declarative constraints (@NotNull, @Size, @DecimalMin) checked at a boundary, with class-level constraints for cross-field rules. Pydantic (2017, rewritten in Rust for version 2 in 2023) brought the same idea to Python type hints.

Alexis King's essay "Parse, don't validate" (2019) sharpened it. At the boundary, convert untyped input into a type that can't represent invalid states, so the rest of the program never re-checks. That is exactly what Invoice.model_validate(...) does with model output.
29180a6191:
Constrained decoding. Researchers had constrained sequence generation to grammars for years. The practical tools arrived in 2023: llama.cpp's GBNF grammars, Microsoft's Guidance, and the Outlines library, which compiles a JSON Schema or regex into a finite-state machine that masks invalid tokens.

Function calling (OpenAI, June 2023; Anthropic tool use, 2024) made "the model fills in a JSON object for a declared function" the default way to get structure from hosted models. At first it came without a hard guarantee.

Anthropic added structured outputs, both JSON outputs and strict tool use, with grammar-constrained sampling in late 2025. The deprecated beta header is dated 2025-11-13. Later the parameter moved to output_config.format and the beta header was dropped.
650be5c400:
Verification and calibration. Double-entry bookkeeping is the original cross-field check. Two independent records of the same fact must agree, and a mismatch is investigated, not averaged away.

Calibration comes from weather forecasting (Brier score, 1950). It requires that a forecaster's stated 90% events happen 90% of the time. Language models are known to state confidence that doesn't match their accuracy. So the old tool applies: measure stated confidence against outcomes on labelled data.
22f1edc417: A language model emits one token at a time, each sampled from a probability distribution over its vocabulary (chapter 13). Nothing in plain sampling knows about JSON, your schema or the invoice in front of it. So three different questions can have three different answers for the same response. Each question is answered by a different mechanism.
262a805159:
Syntax asks whether the text parses. Classic failures are a preamble ("Here is the JSON:"), a Markdown code fence, a trailing comma, an unescaped quote inside a string, and truncation at max_tokens that leaves an object unclosed.

Schema asks whether the parsed value has the fields and types you declared. Failures look like "amount": "about $40" where a decimal string was expected, a missing currency, a category outside the enum, or an extra key the consumer doesn't know.

Semantics asks whether the values are correct. Think of a total that doesn't equal the sum of the lines, a due date copied from the previous invoice in the same PDF, or a purchase order number that matches the pattern and doesn't exist.
e1c5bc6db9:
The first two can be guaranteed by construction. Suppose the decoder may only produce tokens that keep the output inside a grammar derived from your schema. Then the result parses and matches the schema, and there is nothing to detect.

The third can't be guaranteed by any decoding trick. Correctness is a relation between the output and the world (the source document, your purchasing system, arithmetic), and the decoder doesn't see the world.

You know the same split from a Spring controller. Jackson proves the request body is well-formed JSON of the right shape. @Valid proves constraints. The service layer still has to check that the account exists and belongs to the caller.
53c3e7b048:
In practice, this changes where failures live. Before structured outputs, most visible extraction failures were parse errors, and parse errors are loud. With structured outputs, parse errors on a completed response mostly disappear. The failures that remain are the quiet ones: well-formed, schema-valid, plausible, wrong.

Teams that used "parse success rate" as their quality metric watch it reach 100% and conclude the problem is solved. That is the trap the exam tests. Example 01_three_properties.py runs four candidate outputs through the three layers, and each layer catches exactly one of them.
94caecf01d: There are four ways to get structured data out of Claude. They differ in what is guaranteed, where the data appears in the response, and which other features they combine with. Once you know the ladder, you can answer most "the JSON is sometimes broken" questions by pointing one rung up.
bd8d81a36a:
JSON outputs and strict tool use are the same mechanism, pointed at different parts of the response. The docs describe them as solving different problems. JSON outputs control what Claude says; strict tool use validates how Claude calls your functions. The two can be combined in one request.

Both are supported on the current lineup (Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5) and on most of the 4.5-and-later models, on the Claude API and most cloud platforms. The docs list exceptions per platform, so check the supported-models list before you depend on it in a new deployment.
7ddda455e6:
The two weaker rungs still matter.

Some features can't be combined with JSON outputs. The documented one is citations, which returns a 400 when enabled together with output_config.format. If you need both cited prose and structure, you have two choices. Ask for structure in tags and parse defensively (section 12), or run two calls.

And the prompt rung is still the right tool when the output is mostly prose for a human, with only a small machine-read part. A support reply with a trailing routing tag is the typical case.
e207747466: One rung has been removed. Older guides taught prefill: end the request with an assistant turn containing {, so the model continues inside a JSON object. Prefill returns a 400 on Claude 4.6 and later models, including Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 (chapter 05). The structured-outputs page also lists it as incompatible with JSON outputs. So if an exam option proposes prefill as the fix for malformed JSON on a current model, it is wrong twice over.
3a76c50377:
To see what the guarantee covers, look at one decoding step. The model computes a score for every token in its vocabulary, given everything so far. Normally the API samples from those scores.

With a schema, the API first compiles the schema into a grammar. In effect, that's a state machine that knows which characters may come next at each position. At each step the API masks every token that would leave the grammar: a letter where a digit must go, a key not in properties, a closing brace before a required key has appeared. It samples only from the tokens that remain. The output can't leave the grammar, so it parses and it matches.
1d495e2125:
Three consequences follow directly from the mechanism, and each one is examinable.

First, the mask constrains form, not content. Say the source gives the total as 5,022.00 and the model's scores prefer 5202.00. Both are legal under "pattern": "^\d+(\.\d{1,4})?$", and the decoder happily emits the wrong one.

Second, the mask can force a value where the honest answer is "none". If due_date is required and typed as a string, every token that would express absence is masked at the position where the date goes. The model must write some date. So constrained decoding makes hallucinated fill more likely for fields the schema doesn't allow to be empty. That is why section 09 insists on nullable fields.

Third, the schema has to compile. Some features are expensive or impossible to express as a finite grammar: recursion, numeric ranges, string length bounds, arbitrary array sizes. Those aren't supported. The API also limits how large the combined grammar of a request may be.
be754499dc:
The compile step also explains the operational notes in the docs. The first request with a new schema pays extra latency while the grammar compiles. Compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours from last use. Changing the structure of a schema or the set of tools invalidates that cache. Changing only name or description fields doesn't, so you can iterate on descriptions without paying for recompilation.

Separately, changing output_config.format invalidates the prompt cache for the conversation thread (chapter 15). The API also injects a format prompt that adds input tokens. Neither is a reason to avoid the feature. Both are reasons to keep schemas stable and versioned, like any other contract.
1aea525309: Finally, the grammar applies to Claude's direct output, not to tool results or thinking. The docs say grammars apply only to the direct output, not to tool use calls, tool results or thinking. For tool calls, you get the same guarantee by marking the tool strict. That's why the two features exist side by side.
b6462ef910:
The current request parameter is output_config.format, with "type": "json_schema" and a schema object.

An older top-level parameter, output_format, is deprecated. The docs say it has moved to output_config.format and that beta headers are no longer required. The old name only works with the structured-outputs-2025-11-13 beta header; without it, you get a 400. The Python SDK from version 1.0 raises a TypeError if you pass output_format to messages.create. If you see code or an exam option with output_format on the raw API, read it as legacy.
31cd81443d:
Read the answer from the text block by type, not by position. A response can carry other blocks, thinking for example. Code that reads content[0].text breaks the day you turn thinking on; chapter 12 has that incident.

The json.loads on the last line can't fail when stop_reason is end_turn. It still belongs inside your validation layer, though. The same code path will one day receive a truncated or refused response, if someone removes the check above.
39d4eba455:
The SDKs add a typed path. In Python, client.messages.parse() takes a Pydantic model. (The SDK argument is also called output_format, but that's a client-side convenience, not the deprecated API field.) It converts the model to a schema, sends it as output_config.format, validates the response, and returns the instance in response.parsed_output. The docs call this the recommended method.

The conversion step matters. The SDK:

  • removes constraints the decoder doesn't support (minimum, maxLength and similar);
  • copies them into the field description, so the model still sees them;
  • adds additionalProperties: false;
  • filters string formats to the supported list;
  • validates the original constraints on the way back, since it still has the original model.

A transform_schema() helper returns the transformed schema without sending a request. Treat exact helper names as version-specific and check the SDK docs for your version. What matters is the pattern: the decoder enforces the subset, and the validator enforces the rest.
2a617e510a: Property order. Required properties come first, then optional ones, each group in schema order. If a downstream consumer or a human reader depends on order, make every property required (and nullable where needed). That also keeps every key present, which simplifies consumers.
3a270b0a60: Enum capitalisation. The docs note that enum and const values may, rarely, differ from the schema only in capitalisation, while the response completes normally. Typically it's the first letter of a word after a space. Compare enum values case-insensitively, and don't define two values that differ only in case. Example 12_enum_unclear_other.py includes the normalising comparison.
9edf39e99a: Incompatibilities. Citations with output_config.format is a 400, and prefill is incompatible. Batch processing, token counting, streaming and combining with strict tools are all compatible. So an overnight extraction job can use JSON outputs at the batch discount (chapter 07).
1ccd49a387: Data handling. The schema itself is cached, for grammar compilation, for up to 24 hours since last use. The docs say structured outputs are HIPAA eligible, but PHI must not appear in schema definitions: not in property names, enum values, const values or pattern regexes. A schema with an enum of patient names, or a pattern built from a member ID, is a compliance defect, not a style issue.
d12ca099d9: For the Java reader, the request is the same JSON. With the Anthropic Java SDK you build it with the SDK's builders; the output-config builder names are SDK-version specific, so check the Java SDK docs. With a plain HTTP client you post the same body. What matters on the JVM side is the reading path. Deserialize the text block with Jackson into a record annotated for Bean Validation, then validate (section 10).
7761e127d4: Because the schema becomes a grammar, only part of JSON Schema is supported. The list below comes from the structured-outputs documentation as of October 2026. It has changed between releases, so treat it as the shape of the rule and check the page before relying on an edge. An unsupported feature returns a 400 with details. That's the good outcome: you find out at the first request, not in production data.
8ca4e5eb79:
Then there are complexity limits. They are combined across every strict schema in one request, meaning the JSON output schema plus every tool marked strict:

  • at most 20 strict tools per request (non-strict tools don't count);
  • at most 24 optional parameters (every property not listed in required);
  • at most 16 union-type parameters (anyOf or type arrays).

Beyond those counts there is an internal grammar-size limit, which returns 400 "Schema is too complex for compilation". There is also a compilation timeout of 180 seconds.
42baa1ab9f:
The limits interact with the design advice in section 09. The cleanest way to allow absence is "required key, nullable value", written as {"anyOf": [{"type": "string"}, {"type": "null"}]}. That doesn't count against the 24 optional parameters. But each one counts as a union against the 16. So a 40-field extraction schema where every field may be absent breaks one limit or the other, whichever way you write it.

The fixes are structural:

  • split the extraction into two calls, by section of the document;
  • group related nullable fields into one nullable object (one union instead of five);
  • make some fields non-null strings with an explicit sentinel, but only where a sentinel is unambiguous.

Example 04_schema_limits.py shows a 30-field schema failing on optional count, then on union count after the obvious rewrite.
e22dd49689:
The rows marked "not supported" aren't lost. They move to the validator. A severity between 1 and 4 becomes "type": "integer" in the schema, with the range in the description so the model sees it. In Pydantic it becomes Field(ge=1, le=4), and in Bean Validation @Min(1) @Max(4).

The SDK transformation does this automatically, and example 03_pydantic_to_schema.py reimplements it. The raw Pydantic schema fails a local lint for maxLength, minimum and maximum. The transformed schema passes. And a response with severity: 9 is still rejected after decoding.
b2c405a0c5:
You enable strict tool use by setting "strict": true as a top-level property of a tool definition, next to name, description and input_schema. The documented guarantees are two. The tool input strictly follows the input_schema, and the tool name is always valid.

Its main purpose is agents that call real functions. A passengers field declared as an integer arrives as 2, never "2" or "two", so your dispatcher no longer needs coercion code. The tool implementation side, including error results and approval, is chapter 21.
a1b6004518:
The older and still common pattern is tool use as extraction. You declare a tool that you never execute, whose input_schema is your output schema, and you read the extraction from the tool_use block.

It predates JSON outputs. Before strict mode, it was the most reliable way to get schema-shaped output. That's why CCAR-F task statement 4.3 says tool use with JSON schemas is the most reliable way to get schema-compliant output, while still allowing semantic errors.

Today you choose between it and JSON outputs on fit. Use JSON outputs when the whole answer is the data and nothing else happens in the conversation. Use an extraction tool in three cases:

  • the extraction is one step in a tool-using conversation (the agent looks up the customer, then records a structured case);
  • you want several typed records in one response (several tool_use blocks, or one call with an array);
  • the model should pick a different schema per document type, from several extraction tools.
7c164ec479:
The control knob for the extraction tool is tool_choice (chapter 05). auto lets the model decide whether to call a tool. any forces some tool call. {"type": "tool", "name": "record_invoice"} forces that tool. none forbids tools.

Forcing was the classic way to guarantee the extraction path. On the current flagship models it is restricted. Forced tool choice isn't available with manual extended thinking on any model. The docs also state that Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 reject forced tool_choice, and recommend auto with strict tool use or JSON outputs instead. (Chapter 05 verified this; check the docs for the model you deploy.)

So on those models the extraction tool pattern becomes: a strict tool, tool_choice: auto, a system prompt that says to answer by calling the tool, and code that handles the case where the model replied in text instead. If you need a hard guarantee that the answer is structured, JSON outputs gives you one without any tool choice at all.
00ecec1fe8:
Teams get three details in that code wrong.

The stop_reason check comes first. With auto the model may answer in prose, and a parser that searches the prose for numbers is how hallucinated fields enter the database.

The call count is checked, because nothing in the schema says "exactly one call per response". Show the model a two-page PDF with a credit note on page two, and it may reasonably record two invoices.

And the tool's input still goes through Pydantic and the business rules. Strict mode delivers a valid shape, not a valid invoice.

Don't send a tool_result back for an extraction tool unless the conversation continues. If it does, every tool_use id needs a matching tool_result in the next user turn (chapter 05).
276d32495d: Most semantic errors in extraction aren't misreadings. They are the model doing what the schema asked: producing a value for a field the document doesn't support. Section 05 explained why constrained decoding makes this worse when absence isn't legal. Schema design is the cheapest semantic control you have, because it changes what a correct answer can look like.
1a61cbce49:
For every field a real document may lack, allow null, and say in the description exactly what null means.

Prefer "required key, nullable value" to "optional key". Both allow absence. But required-nullable keeps every key present, so consumers never have to tell "missing key" from "null". It also keeps property order stable, and it doesn't count toward the 24-optional limit. Optional keys are still fine for genuinely optional sub-objects.

CCAR-F 4.3 phrases the same rule as "optional fields for missing information". Whichever syntax you use, the exam is testing one idea: the schema must allow the model not to answer.
2f51fb9866:
Write the description as an instruction about the source, not the field: "Payment due date as printed. null if the document shows none. Do not compute it from payment terms."

That last sentence matters. Without it, a model that sees "Net 30" will often compute a due date. It's a reasonable inference and a wrong extraction, because your accounts-payable system may apply a different calendar. If you want derived values, derive them in code from extracted inputs, where the rule is visible and testable.
aa78cdcd4b: Example 13_nullable_fields.py is a seeded simulation, not a model run. Still, it shows the shape you see in real evaluations. On 71 documents with no due date, the non-nullable schema produces 71 invented dates, and the nullable one produces 3. That residual 3 is why nullable fields don't replace grounding checks (section 16).
ceb85d0b0b:
A closed enum has the same problem in another form. Say intent must be one of billing, outage, port_in, device. A message that mentions both an outage and a bill gets one of the four labels, confidently. So does a message in a language you didn't expect, and a request you never anticipated ("can you recycle my old router?").

Add two values with distinct meanings:

  • unclear means the input doesn't support a single label: ambiguous, multi-intent, garbled.
  • other means the input clearly belongs to a category you didn't list. It must be paired with a free-text other_detail field that says what it is.

The pairing is a cross-field rule: detail required when other, null otherwise. The schema can't express that directly, so it goes in the validator.
e95f0a44f6:
The two values are routed differently, which is why they must not be merged. unclear goes to a human or a clarifying question, because the input is the problem. other is accepted with its detail, and the details are counted. When "device recycling" shows up 400 times a month, that's a new category to add. It becomes a product decision driven by data, rather than a model forcing it into device.

Example 12_enum_unclear_other.py runs five messages through a closed and an open enum. The closed enum gets two of five right, the open one five, and the open one reports the new category it found.
c3d4873604:
Decide the canonical form of every value in the schema, and enforce it in code. Dates are ISO 8601 ("format": "date"). Money is a decimal string with no symbol, plus a separate currency enum. Phone numbers are E.164. Identifiers keep their printed form.

Tell the model the target format in the description, and also normalise in code. The decoder guarantees the pattern, not that the model mapped the source to it correctly.

The classic case is 03/04/2026. The pattern accepts either reading, so the model's choice between March 4 and April 3 is a guess. That changes only if the description fixes the convention or other dates in the source disambiguate. Normalisation code should reject ambiguity rather than guess, as 17_normalisation.py does.
a9ff7dd515: Money deserves its own rule. Don't ask for money as a JSON number. Binary floating point can't represent most decimal amounts exactly (0.1 + 0.2 prints 0.30000000000000004), and different consumers round differently. Ask for a decimal string with a pattern, and parse it into Decimal or BigDecimal. That also makes the cross-field arithmetic in section 11 exact.
722af69d9b: Ask for what is printed, compute in code. Extract stated_total, line quantities and unit prices, then compute the calculated total yourself. Asking the model to "calculate the total" mixes reading with arithmetic, and hides which one failed.
4277298d96: Descriptions are instructions. The model reads property descriptions. Put the extraction rule there ("as printed", "null if absent", "do not infer"). Don't put it in a separate paragraph of the system prompt that the model must map to fields.
24d435e198: Add fields that make review cheaper. Consider a quote per important field (section 16), a detected_pattern on findings (section 16), and a notes field for anything the schema couldn't hold. Each costs tokens and saves reviewer minutes.
05fc9f35a6:
Validation is a sequence of layers. Each layer answers one question with a typed failure.

The order matters. There's no point running arithmetic on a value that isn't a number. And each layer's failure goes to a different place: retry, review, or dead letter.

A Spring developer has built this many times, as a filter chain or a chain of validators behind a controller. The only change is that the client is a model, and your response to a failure can include telling it what was wrong.
8af24a6aa8: Layers 0 to 2 are generic, and should be the same code for every model call in the service. Layers 3 to 6 are per use case, and that's where the domain knowledge lives. Keeping the generic part in one place keeps the per-use-case part small enough to test well.
3798dd670d:
Pydantic version 2 gives you types, field constraints and model-level validators in one class. Use Decimal for money, date for dates and Literal for enums. For required-nullable fields, use Optional[...] without a default; Pydantic then requires the key and allows None.

Keep the business rules in a separate function or a model_validator(mode="after"). A separate function is easier to test, and it lets you return all rule failures at once instead of only the first.
e4513afd41:
Each rule returns a code and a message. The code drives routing; section 17 decides retry or review by code. The message has two readers. One is the model, because the message may be sent back in a retry turn (section 14). The other is a human reviewer.

Write messages that state the observed values and the expected relation, as above, not "validation failed". Example 06_validation_layers.py runs six variants of the invoice through the layers and prints which layer caught each.
641c48d978:
On the JVM, the same layers map to familiar tools. Jackson handles parse and types. Jakarta Bean Validation handles field constraints. A class-level constraint or a service method handles cross-field rules. A repository lookup handles reference data.

Three Jackson settings matter for model output:

  • keep FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES on, because an unexpected key means the schema and the code disagree;
  • turn on USE_BIG_DECIMAL_FOR_FLOATS if any money arrives as a number;
  • turn off coercion of scalars (ACCEPT_FLOAT_AS_INT and the coercion config for strings to numbers), so a type mismatch fails instead of being silently converted.

Records with compact constructors suit the "parse, don't validate" style well. Once constructed, the object is valid.
110d16e4cb:
Reference-data checks (does PO-7781 exist, is this customer ours) don't belong in a constraint annotation. They need a repository and a transaction. Put them in the service that consumes the validated record. Give them the same code-plus-message failure shape, so the router treats them uniformly.

One trap: the @PastOrPresent annotation uses the JVM clock. In tests, inject a Clock through a custom constraint instead. Otherwise the test that passes today fails next year.
56082c0fce:
For documents with numbers, the single most useful semantic check is to extract the same fact twice and compare in code: once as stated, once as derivable from other fields.

An invoice states a subtotal, a tax and a total. It also lists lines with quantities and unit prices. If the model misreads one digit anywhere, the stated and calculated values disagree. You learn about the error without knowing the right answer.

This is double-entry bookkeeping applied to extraction. CCAR-F 4.4 names it explicitly ("calculated vs stated totals").
d4c226f370:
The rule for the prompt is: transcribe, don't compute. Ask for stated_total as printed, and for the line values as printed. Code computes calculated_total.

Suppose you ask the model for the total and let it add. A misread line and a "corrected" total can then agree with each other and disagree with the document. The check you relied on is gone.

Some teams put both a stated_total and a calculated_total in the schema, so the model's own arithmetic is visible. That's fine, as long as code recomputes and compares rather than trusting either.
5c9cdd336a:
A mismatch has three possible causes, and each is handled differently.

  • A misread: the model wrote 5202.00 for 5,022.00, or dropped a line. A second reading, with the specific discrepancy pointed out, can fix it, so it's retryable once.
  • An error in the document: the vendor's own arithmetic is wrong, which happens on real invoices. No reading can fix that. A retry either returns the same faithful extraction or, worse, "corrects" the document so the numbers agree. It goes to a human, with both values shown.
  • A convention: tax-inclusive line prices, rounding per line versus per total, discounts printed as negative lines. You encode it once as a rule, with a tolerance, after seeing it in data.
49eb89e8af:
Note the "line dropped" case. The stated subtotal is what exposes a missing line. Had you asked the model only for lines and computed the subtotal yourself, a dropped line would produce a self-consistent, wrong invoice.

Redundancy in the source is what makes the check work. So extract the redundant fields even when your downstream system doesn't need them. The idea goes beyond invoices. A call-detail summary states "42 calls, 318 minutes" next to a list of calls. A contract states a term in months and gives start and end dates. A network ticket's affected-site count should match the listed sites.
57141dabb4:
You still parse free text in four situations:

  • citations are on (incompatible with JSON outputs);
  • a platform or older model lacks structured outputs;
  • the output is mostly prose with a machine-read part;
  • you consume output from systems you don't control (another team's agent, a Claude Code run with plain-text output).

Defensive parsing is the discipline of extracting exactly the value you agreed on, and refusing everything else loudly.
312b70e797:
The agreement comes first. Ask for the structured part inside a delimiter, for example <json>...</json> or <route>billing</route>. Give one example of the full output in the prompt (chapter 17). Then parse by the delimiter.

Without a delimiter, extraction degenerates into guessing which brace starts the object. The classic regex \{.*\} fails on a brace inside a string, on two objects in one reply, and on truncated output. In each case it returns something rather than failing.
0ceebb269d: For JSON inside text, Python's json.JSONDecoder().raw_decode(s, i) parses one complete value starting at position i and returns where it ended. So you can scan to the first { or [, decode exactly one value, and report any trailing text. Jackson's equivalent is a JsonParser over the substring: read one tree, then check nextToken(). Neither guesses. An unclosed object is an error.
5d321d5dcf:
A few short rules separate defensive parsing from optimistic parsing.

  • Repair only what is unambiguous: stripping a Markdown fence is safe. Replacing single quotes, removing trailing commas or closing open brackets changes meaning or hides truncation.
  • Surface what you ignored: report trailing text and second objects rather than dropping them silently. "Two objects" may mean the model extracted two invoices.
  • Validate after parsing exactly as you would for structured output: the parsed value goes through the same layers 2 to 6.
  • Log the raw text on every failure, with the request id, so the failure can be replayed (chapter 12).

And if parse failures on this path exceed a small rate, move up the ladder in section 04. Don't grow the repair function.
06c387f327: There's one more reason not to "repair" model JSON with lenient parsers, such as JSON5 or a library that auto-closes brackets. A truncated response that has been auto-closed is schema-valid and incomplete. The invoice with its last three lines cut off becomes an invoice with fewer lines. Only the totals check (section 11) has a chance of noticing. Truncation is a stop_reason problem, handled before parsing.
84fccf6145:
Every structured-output guarantee depends on the response having completed normally. The structured-outputs page is explicit about the two exceptions.

On a refusal, the response has stop_reason: "refusal" with HTTP 200, and you are billed for generated tokens. "The refusal message takes precedence over schema constraints", so the text may be a sentence, not JSON.

On max_tokens, the output "may be incomplete and not match your schema".

Both arrive as successful HTTP responses, so a generic error handler never sees them. The output handler must check stop_reason before it parses anything.
b968a340f3:
Chapter 12 (section 07) covers the general recovery for both: continuation for truncated prose, fallback to another model once for refusals, streaming retraction, and batch items that report refusals as succeeded. Here only the structured-output specifics matter:

  • A truncated JSON output is never continued and stitched together. Raise max_tokens, or shrink the output (fewer fields, split the document), and run again.
  • A truncated tool_use block is never executed.
  • A refusal is not retried on the same model in a loop. It goes to a fallback model once, or to review.

The docs add one more case. Asking for the model's reasoning inside structured output can trigger a refusal categorised as reasoning extraction. They suggest asking for a short explanation instead. If your schema has a reasoning field and you see refusals, change that first.
8b200de201:
The default branch raises. New stop reasons appear over time: model_context_window_exceeded and pause_turn both arrived after many integrations were written. An output handler that treats "anything else" as success will parse whatever text happens to be there.

Note the max_tokens row too. The naive parser failed loudly here only because the cut happened mid-string. Cut at a different point, and a lenient parser produces a shorter, valid-looking object.

Sizing max_tokens for structured output is arithmetic. Estimate the largest legitimate output (lines times tokens per line, plus overhead) and add margin. Then alert when the observed max_tokens rate exceeds a small threshold, because it means your documents have grown.
aeaaf03a02:
When validation fails, the cheapest fix that works is often a second attempt. In it, the model sees its own previous output and the specific errors.

That's different from a blind retry. A blind retry re-sends the same request and hopes sampling lands somewhere else. For a systematic misreading, it reproduces the same mistake. And on the newest models you can't even vary sampling parameters (chapter 05).

A feedback retry changes the input. It adds information the first attempt didn't have: which check failed, and with what values.
a66e185c16:
The mechanics are a conversation. Keep the original user turn. Append the failed output as an assistant turn. Then append a user turn that does four things:

  • lists the errors exactly as the validator produced them;
  • asks for a corrected extraction;
  • says to change only what the errors require;
  • restates the escape hatch ("if a value is not printed, use null rather than guessing").

That last sentence isn't decoration. Without it, an error message like "po_number: required" reads as an instruction to produce a PO number, and a cooperative model will produce one (section 15).
5ba9fe7ae7:
Four design decisions make the loop safe in production.

  • Bound it: one or two retries. Data from real pipelines tends to show most of the benefit in the first retry and little after. Each retry also re-sends the whole document.
  • Stop on repetition: if the same error comes back, the model isn't converging. Further attempts cost money without changing the outcome.
  • Retry only retryable codes: section 15 sorts errors into those a re-read can fix and those it can't, and the router consults that list.
  • Record attempts: the audit record for a document should show every attempt and its errors. "Accepted after one retry" is a quality signal you'll want to measure. A rising retry rate after a model or prompt change is an early warning.
7972f6e3e1:
Two variants are worth knowing.

With an extraction tool, the feedback goes back as a tool_result with is_error: true for the tool_use id, containing the validation errors. That keeps the protocol well formed. It's the same shape your agent uses for any tool failure (chapter 21).

With prompt caching (chapter 15), put the document in a cached prefix. The retry then pays the cache-read price for it, and the retry turns at the end are the only new tokens.

In Java the loop is the same. Spring Retry's RetryTemplate is a poor fit, though, because it re-invokes the same call. This loop changes the request each time, so write it explicitly or use a small state machine.
e3237a7e30:
Retry with feedback works when the information needed to pass the check is in the input and the model missed it. It can't work when the information isn't there. Think of a torn scan with the PO box illegible, a contract that never states a renewal date, or a support message that doesn't mention the account number. No number of re-readings will find a value that doesn't exist.

Worse, a retry loop with a validator that demands the value creates pressure. The model can relieve it only by inventing a value, and the loop then reports success. CCAR-F 4.4 states the rule directly: retries fail when the information is absent from the source.
bfcaf023e2:
Example 10_when_retry_cannot_help.py makes that concrete. The validator requires a non-null po_number, and the document has none. The fake model returns null twice. On the third attempt, under the repeated "po_number: required" message, it returns PO-7718. That value matches the pattern and isn't in the purchasing system. The loop reports a valid record after three calls.

The fixed version makes null legal. It classifies the absence as "missing in source", detected from the illegible marker, and routes the document to review after one call.
b78fb48b73: The general tool: classify every validation code by whether a re-read can fix it, and route the rest. The table below is a starting point for an extraction pipeline. Your own codes will differ, but the column that matters is the second.
378bdce79b:
The reference-lookup row deserves emphasis, because it's the most common mistake in practice. Feed "PO-4410 not found in purchasing system" back to the model, and you invite it to produce a PO that is in the system. If your prompt or tools expose the list of valid POs, it may pick a plausible one. The validator has become an oracle the model can satisfy without reading the document.

Lookups are checks on the world. Their failures go to people or to reconciliation processes, not back to the model.
aa0218ff27:
CCAR-F also lists a detected_pattern field in this context. Sometimes a model produces findings rather than extractions: suspicious charges, code-review issues, policy violations. Then false positives are the dominant failure. They can't be retried away either, because each individual finding looks plausible.

So ask the model to label each finding with the pattern it believes it detected, from an enum. Reviewer dismissals then become data. Group dismissals by pattern, and the worst pattern stands out.

Example 19_detected_pattern.py shows a pipeline at 50% overall precision. One pattern (round_number_amount) is at 10%, and the others at 90%. The fix is to remove or tighten that one pattern's criteria (chapter 17), not to tell the model to "be more careful" across the board.
d35729b50a:
The last item in objective 6.3 is about attitude, backed by mechanism.

A language model's output is fluent by construction. It's grammatical, well formatted, in a confident register, and with structured outputs it's perfectly shaped. None of those properties correlates reliably with correctness. The model is trained to produce fluency on every input. Correctness depends on whether the answer was in the input or the training data, and whether the model used it.

A human reader takes fluency as a sign of competence, because for human writers it usually is. For model output that heuristic misleads. The engineering response is to verify claims by means that don't depend on how the claim was phrased.
571c13f1ad:
Three mechanisms make confident errors likely in output handling specifically.

  • forced completeness: a schema that requires a value produces one, as section 05 showed.
  • plausible-pattern completion: an ID with a known format, a date near other dates, a total near other totals. These are exactly what a next-token predictor produces when the evidence is weak.
  • self-consistency: within one response, the model tends to make later values agree with earlier ones. A misread early value propagates, and the output agrees with itself while disagreeing with the source.

That last one is why cross-checks within one model's output help only when the inputs to the check were transcribed separately (section 11).
a3262cec91:
A tempting design adds a confidence field (0 to 1) to the schema and routes low-confidence records to review. But the number comes from the same process as the answer. It's a token sequence the model judged plausible in context, not a measured probability of correctness.

Models tend to report high confidence across the board. The errors that matter most often come with high stated confidence. Use the number as the only gate, and most errors land in the "auto-accept" bucket.
23940be8e4:
If you want to use a stated confidence at all, treat it like any uncalibrated score. Collect a labelled set. Bucket by stated confidence and measure actual accuracy per bucket. Pick a threshold from the measured curve, per field and per document type. Then re-measure after every model or prompt change.

Example 16_confidence_uncalibrated.py is a seeded simulation of what that measurement typically reveals. The 0.99 bucket is right 90% of the time, and the 0.80 bucket 63%. And 53 of 91 errors sit in the buckets stated at 0.95 or above. Deterministic checks (totals, grounding, lookups) flag more of the errors than the number does, whatever the model said about itself.

CCAR-F 4.6 makes a related point about self-review. A model reviewing its own output in the same context keeps its generation reasoning and tends to confirm it. Verification belongs in an independent pass.
a3c5359f1b:
A verification pass is a second, independent model call whose job is to check, not to produce. It receives the source and the candidate fields, not the first call's reasoning. It returns a verdict per field (supported, contradicted, not_found) along with the exact source text it relied on.

Independence is the point. A fresh context doesn't carry the first pass's misreading forward. Use a different prompt, and consider a different model. A cheaper model is often enough for checking, because checking a stated value against a quoted span is easier than finding it.
7328d38ea6:
Three rules keep verification honest.

  • The verifier does not correct. If it rewrote values, you would have two unverified extractions and no way to choose. Disagreement routes to review.
  • The verifier's own output is checked mechanically. Its evidence quotes must occur in the source (next subsection). Otherwise the verifier is just a second confident voice.
  • Verification is targeted. Run it on fields where an error is expensive (amounts, dates, identifiers), or on high-value records that passed the rules. Don't run it on everything, because it roughly doubles the cost of the fields it covers.

Example 14_verification_pass.py catches a transposed total that passed every schema check.
f397c967f2:
Grounding asks for evidence alongside each important value, and checks the evidence in code. In a JSON output, each field becomes a pair {value, quote}, where quote is a verbatim span of the source. Code then checks two things. Does the quote occur in the source, after whitespace and case normalisation? And can the value be derived from the quote? (The digits of 5022.00 appear in "TOTAL USD 5,022.00".) A value with no locatable quote is unsupported, however confident it looks.

This is cheap and deterministic. It catches the three most common confident errors:

  • invented values (no quote);
  • paraphrased evidence (quote not in source);
  • misread values with a correct quote (value not in quote).
61abdb3df9:
For free-text answers, the API's citations feature does the same job natively. You pass documents with citations enabled, and the response's text blocks carry citation objects that point at spans of the source.

Citations can't be combined with output_config.format, so you choose per use case. Use citations for cited prose answers, such as a support reply that quotes the tariff. Use the quote-per-field pattern for JSON extraction. The exam-relevant point: a citation or quote is only worth something if code checks it.
f9b09f6141: Here is the whole chapter as one pipeline. Telecom vendor invoices arrive as text, either OCR output or PDF text. Each must end in one of three places: an accepted record in accounts payable, a review task with a reason, or a requeue with a fix. The running example lives in invoice_model.py and 18_pipeline_end_to_end.py. The design decisions, in order:
11bf641de9: Schema. Every key is required. Values are nullable where a real invoice may lack them (due_date, po_number, category_other_detail). The category enum includes other and unclear. Money is a decimal string with a pattern, dates use format: date, and additionalProperties: false applies everywhere. CI lints it locally against the supported subset and limits (three unions, zero optional parameters).
ad60ec733e: Request. JSON outputs via output_config.format, because the whole answer is data and no tools are involved. The system prompt says "exactly as printed, null for absent fields". The document sits inside <invoice> tags in a cached prefix, and max_tokens is sized from the longest invoice seen, plus margin. Model choice comes from evaluation: Haiku 5.5 may be enough for clean OCR, Sonnet 5.5 for noisy scans (chapter 15 covers the cost side).
fda563d588: Retry policy. One feedback retry, and only if every failing code is in the retryable set (SUBTOTAL, TOTAL, LINE_MATH). PO_UNKNOWN, DATES and FUTURE route straight to review.
cf3d63fb2c: Grounding and verification for the amount fields on invoices above an approval threshold. The companion's pipeline omits them to stay readable; examples 14 and 15 implement them.
fe1dae17f4:
Walk the six rows, because each one exercises a different branch.

  • inv-1 passes every layer on the first call.
  • inv-2 dropped a line on the first read. The stated subtotal exposed it. The code SUBTOTAL is retryable, the feedback turn named the discrepancy, and the second read was correct.
  • inv-3 has a PO number that is read correctly but unknown to purchasing. That isn't retryable, so it goes to review on the first call, without asking the model to "find a valid PO".
  • inv-4 hit max_tokens. Nothing was parsed, and the job is requeued with a larger cap. In a batch pipeline, such jobs are collected and resubmitted together (chapter 07).
  • inv-5 was refused, so it goes to review. If refusals cluster on a document type, that's a prompt or model question for chapter 12's fallback policy.
  • inv-6 twice reported a total that disagrees with its own lines. After one retry with the same error, the evidence says a re-read won't help. It goes to review with both numbers, where a person will find either a misread or a vendor error.
b1b75a820b:
Eight calls for six documents is the cost of this policy: two retries.

In a real pipeline you would watch three numbers from the audit records: the accept rate, the retry rate (accepted after a retry), and the review rate by reason. A model upgrade, a prompt change or a new vendor template moves those numbers before anyone notices individual errors.

The Java version of this pipeline has the same shape. It uses a sealed interface Outcome permits Accept, Review, Requeue, a switch on stop_reason, Jackson plus the validator from section 10, and the same retryable-code set.
7fba89b1cb:
Output handling has two kinds of tests, matching chapter 12's two layers.

The deterministic kind tests your code. It checks that:

  • the schema is in the supported subset, and every key is required;
  • each business rule fires on a crafted bad record and stays quiet on a good one;
  • the stop gate raises for every non-success stop_reason;
  • the retry loop stops on repetition and never retries a non-retryable code.

These run in CI without a model, against fakes. See example 20_test_suite.py, and the strict fake in out_fake.py, which also rejects output_format and citations with JSON outputs. They should never be flaky.
bc2329471a:
The statistical kind measures the model with your schema and prompt. It covers:

  • field-level accuracy on a labelled set of documents, per field, because "98% of records correct" hides that due_date is right 80% of the time;
  • the null-precision of nullable fields: when the model says null, is the field really absent, and when the field is absent, does the model say null;
  • enum confusion, including unclear and other;
  • the operational rates from section 17.

Run it before any change to model, prompt or schema, and compare against the last run. A schema change is a prompt change, because the descriptions are instructions.
1919e76827: Labelled sets for extraction are cheaper to build than they sound. Start from the review queue. Every document a person corrected is a labelled example with a known hard case. Add a stratified sample of accepted documents, labelled once by a person. Fifty documents per template catch large regressions. A few hundred let you see per-field changes of a few points.
18c84715d5: The failure is syntax, and constrained decoding guarantees syntax. A lowers the rate without guaranteeing anything. C returns a 400 on 4.6+ models such as Sonnet 5.5, and it's incompatible with JSON outputs. D is optimistic parsing that fails on braces in strings and on two objects. B also keeps the two checks the guarantee doesn't cover: stop_reason (refusal or truncation) and value validation.
29fcf824e5: Strict mode guarantees shape, not values, so this is a semantic error. Calculated-versus-stated reconciliation detects misreads without ground truth. The retry-then-review policy handles both misreads and vendor errors. B relies on uncalibrated self-reported confidence. D can agree on the same misread, since both calls share the same failure tendencies. A may lower the rate but gives no detection.
34780557bd: Retries can't recover information that isn't in the source. Pressure from the validator produces fabricated values, which are the "successes" on attempt four. The schema must allow absence, and absence is routed, not retried. A amplifies both symptoms. C misdiagnoses. D isn't available on the newest models (non-default sampling parameters are rejected), and it wouldn't create missing information anyway.
550a2e97c2: The docs state that Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 reject forced tool choice. They recommend auto with strict tools, or structured outputs (chapter 05; check the docs for your model). B is also a forced choice. A drops the guarantee. D is a 400 on these models. If no other tools are involved, JSON outputs is the simplest way to guarantee the structure.
c96d1a00d4: A closed enum forces a label on ambiguous and out-of-taxonomy inputs. unclear, and other + detail, give both a legal answer, with different routing. A relies on uncalibrated confidence. C grows the taxonomy, but ambiguous or unforeseen messages still have no legal answer. D institutionalises the error.
8d942379bf: Citations and JSON outputs are documented as incompatible. B keeps grounding by moving it into the schema with a code check, or it splits the job. A breaks a requirement of the schema subset. C is deprecated, and it's the same feature anyway. D is a 400 on current models.
6682466169: Same-context self-review keeps the generation reasoning and confirms itself. Stated confidence is uncalibrated too. An independent verifier with mechanically checked evidence is the documented pattern (CCAR-F 4.6). A and C keep the same context. D is unrelated.
828b9feaa7: Extend 05_tool_use_extraction.py so that a document containing two invoices produces two tool_use blocks. Then change the contract check to accept N calls when the source has N invoice headers.
0a8257decb: Add a rule to invoice_model.business_rules: line descriptions containing "credit" must have negative amounts. Add a test for it to 20_test_suite.py, and decide whether its code is retryable.
